Curriculum › Year 5

Year 5: what your child practises

In Year 5, Sharpwise has 38 topics in maths and 15 topics in English. Each one is below in plain words, with ideas to try at home.

Year 5 topics follow the National Curriculum for England. This page is made from the game's own list of topics, so it changes when the game does.

Play Sharpwise

Maths in Year 5

38 topics, grouped by the part of the curriculum each one practises.

Number: number and place value

Place Value to a Million
Read, write, order, compare to 1,000,000; digit value; count in powers of 10
Negative Numbers
Negative numbers in context, count through 0
Round to 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000
Round to 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000, 100,000
Roman Numerals to M
Roman numerals to M; years

Try at home:

  • Make numbers from pairs of playing cards and ask which digit stands for tens and which for ones.

Number: addition and subtraction

Column Adding and Subtracting
More than 4 digits, columnar; round to check
Mental Adding and Subtracting
Mental, increasingly large numbers
Adding and Subtracting Problems
Multi-step problems in context

Try at home:

  • Add the prices of two snacks in your head, then take one away to check the answer.

Number: multiplication and division

Factors and Multiples
Multiples, factor pairs, common factors
Prime Numbers
Primes to 100, prime factors, composite; recall primes to 19
Long Multiplication
Up to 4 digits × 1 or 2 digits, formal methods
Mental Multiplying and Dividing
Mental × and ÷ from known facts
Short Division
Short division up to 4 digits ÷ 1 digit; remainders in context
Times and Divide by 10, 100, 1,000
× and ÷ by 10, 100, 1,000 incl. decimals
Square and Cube Numbers
Square and cube numbers, ² and ³
Balance the Equation
Four operations and the meaning of =
Scaling and Rates Problems
Scaling by simple fractions, simple rates
True or false?
Reason mathematically; multiples, factors, primes, squares and cubes

Try at home:

  • Arrange 12 buttons into equal rows in different ways and see which sizes fit.
  • Set out egg boxes or muffin trays and count the rows and columns to find the lots of.
  • Share a bowl of grapes fairly between family members and ask how many each, and how many are left.
  • Make numbers from pairs of playing cards and ask which digit stands for tens and which for ones.
  • Add the prices of two snacks in your head, then take one away to check the answer.

Number: fractions (including decimals and percentages)

Compare Fractions
Compare and order, related denominators
Equivalent Fractions
Equivalent fractions incl. tenths and hundredths
Mixed Numbers
Mixed numbers and improper fractions
Adding Fractions
Add and subtract, same and related denominators
Fractions Times Whole Numbers
Proper fractions and mixed numbers × whole numbers
Decimals and Fractions
Decimals as fractions, e.g. 0.71 = 71/100
Rounding Decimals
Round 2-dp decimals to the nearest whole and to 1 dp
Thousandths and Decimal Order
Thousandths; order and compare to 3 dp
Per Cent
Per cent; FDP equivalents of 1/2, 1/4, 1/5, 2/5, 4/5, tenths, twenty-fifths

Try at home:

  • Put two heaps of socks or coins side by side and ask which has more, and by how many.
  • Cut a pizza or an apple into equal parts and ask for one half, one quarter or three quarters.
  • Read prices and measurements aloud: say what the digit after the point means, in tenths or hundredths.
  • Spot sale labels and work out one tenth of the price, then a half or a quarter of it.

Measurement

Metric Units and Time
Convert metric units and units of time
Imperial Units
Approximate metric and imperial equivalences
Area and Perimeter
Area of rectangles, composite perimeter, estimating area
Volume and Capacity
Estimate volume and capacity
Measure Problems
Four operations on measures in decimal notation

Try at home:

  • Compare a cup, a jug and a bowl: which holds more? Use a ruler or shoe-lengths to measure the table.

Geometry: properties of shapes

3-D Shapes and Nets
Identify 3-D shapes from 2-D representations
Angles in Degrees
Estimate and compare acute, obtuse and reflex angles
Angle Facts
Angles at a point, on a line, and rectangle facts
Regular Polygons
Regular and irregular polygons

Try at home:

  • Go on a shape hunt around the house for circles, boxes, cylinders and right angles.

Geometry: position and direction

Reflection and Translation
Position after a reflection or translation

Try at home:

  • Go on a shape hunt around the house for circles, boxes, cylinders and right angles.

Statistics

Line Graphs
Comparison, sum and difference from a line graph
Timetables
Read, interpret and complete tables and timetables

Try at home:

  • Tally the cars passing the window or the colours of socks, then say which has most and fewest.
  • Ask what the clock will say in half an hour, then check when the time comes.

English in Year 5

15 topics, grouped by the part of the curriculum each one practises.

Reading: comprehension

Fact or Opinion?
Distinguish between statements of fact and opinion

Try at home:

  • Read a few lines together every day and ask your child to point to the tricky words.

Writing: transcription (spelling)

Year 5–6 Word List (1–50)
Statutory word list, words 1–50
Endings: -cious, -tious, -cial, -tial
Endings which sound like /ʃəs/ and /ʃəl/
Endings: -ant, -ance, -ent, -ence
Words ending in -ant/-ent, -ance/-ence and -ancy/-ency
Endings: -able, -ible, -ably, -ibly
Words ending in -able/-ible and -ably/-ibly
Adding endings to -fer words
Adding suffixes beginning with vowel letters to words ending in -fer
Silent Letters
Words with silent letters (doubt, island, solemn)

Try at home:

  • Choose three words a night: look, cover, write, check, and then say what makes each one tricky.

Writing: vocabulary, grammar and punctuation

Making verbs: -ate, -ise, -ify
Converting nouns or adjectives into verbs using suffixes (-ate, -ise, -ify)
Verb prefixes: dis-, de-, mis-, over-, re-
Verb prefixes dis–, de–, mis–, over– and re–
Relative Clauses
Relative clauses with who, which, where, when, whose, that or an omitted pronoun
Modal Verbs
Degrees of possibility with modal verbs and adverbs
Parenthesis: brackets, dashes, commas
Brackets, dashes or commas to indicate parenthesis
Commas for clear meaning
Commas to clarify meaning or avoid ambiguity
Cohesion: linking adverbials
Linking ideas across paragraphs with adverbials of time, place and number
Perfect tense: had, has, have
The perfect form of verbs to mark relationships of time and cause

Try at home:

  • Look at a favourite book together and spot the full stops, question marks and describing words.
